readerTitle: Your supplier just raised prices 12%. What do you do before you reply?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방 가구 제조사와 경첩 공급사, 소프트웨어 스타트업과 이메일 발송 서비스) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 공급 계약 협상은 가격 숫자 싸움이 아니라, 내 대안을 먼저 계산하고 상대가 가격 뒤에서 정말 원하는 것을 찾아 교환하는 일이다.
misconception: 공급사가 가격을 올리면 '깎아 달라'고 버티거나 중간에서 반씩 양보하는 것 말고는 방법이 없다.

sources.text: 협상론의 표준 개념 (BATNA, 이익과 입장의 구분). Fisher, R. & Ury, W. Getting to Yes (1981)

factChecks.note: 합의안: 5% 인상 $2.10 × 50,000 = $105,000. 제안가 대비 $7,000 절감, 대안 대비 $5,000 절감. 결제 기한 45일→15일 단축은 제조사에게 현금 부담이라는 점을 Watch out 카드에 명시.
소프트웨어 사례의 30% 인상, 2년 계약, 엔지니어 6주 이전 기간은 모두 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Your supplier just raised prices 12%. What do you do before you reply?
body: Mara runs a small kitchen cabinet workshop. She buys 50,000 hinges a year at $2.00 each.
This morning her supplier emailed: from next quarter, $2.24. "Steel costs are up. Please confirm by Friday." Her first instinct is to fire back a firm no.

image.label: Workshop owner reading a price-increase email beside a box of hinges
image.brief: 작은 목공 작업장. 여성 사장이 노트북 화면의 이메일("+12%" 강조)을 보고 있고, 옆 작업대에 경첩 상자가 쌓여 있음. 따뜻한 조명, 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: What should Mara do first?
body: She has until Friday. Which move comes first?

options.text: Reply right away: "We can't accept any increase"
options.feedback: It sounds strong, but she doesn't yet know what happens if they say no. A hard line without a backup is a bluff.

options.text: Get quotes from other suppliers and work out what switching would really cost
options.feedback: This is her **best alternative (BATNA)**. Knowing what she gets if talks fail tells her how hard she can push.

options.text: Accept to protect a good relationship
options.feedback: The relationship matters, but she gives up $12,000 a year without learning if a better deal was possible.

cards.title: Her alternative isn't just the other quote.
body: A second supplier quotes $2.12. But switching means testing samples and adjusting jigs, about $4,000 one time. So her real alternative costs **$2.20 per hinge** in year one. Any deal above that is worse than walking away.

cards.title: A real alternative changes the tone.
body: Mara now knows she can leave and be only a little worse off. She doesn't need to threaten. She can say calmly that she has another option and would prefer to stay.
Notice the alternative is weaker than it first looked. The $2.12 quote alone would have made her overconfident. Counting the switching cost kept her **BATNA** honest.

cards.title: "Steel is up. Twelve percent is final."
body: In the meeting, the sales manager won't move on price. What does Mara say?

options.text: "Match the other quote, or we leave."
options.feedback: Backed by a real alternative, so it's not a bluff. But it's position against position, and it may end a working relationship over a few cents.

options.text: "Help me understand what's driving this. What would make next year easier for you?"
options.feedback: This looks past their **position** (12%) to their **interests**, the needs behind it. Interests can often be met in ways that cost you less than price.
Quick, but she trades without knowing what they need. She may give up more than necessary.

cards.title: The problem wasn't the price.
body: The supplier buys steel months ahead. Late payments and unpredictable orders were squeezing their cash. Mara's real need was a stable cost, because she prints her price list once a year.
They agreed: a 12-month volume commitment with quarterly forecasts, payment in 15 days instead of 45, and **+5% locked for the year**. That's $105,000, below both the offer and her alternative.

image.label: Two sides of a table trading items: forecast, faster payment, locked price
image.brief: 협상 테이블 양쪽에 두 사람. 가운데로 카드 세 장이 오감: "12-month forecast", "Pay in 15 days", "+5% locked". 단순한 플랫 일러스트, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Every trade has a cost.
body: Paying in 15 days means Mara's cash leaves 30 days sooner. She needs to be sure her bank balance can handle it.
A volume commitment is a promise. If orders drop, she may still owe for hinges she can't use. And an alternative only gives you power if you'd truly use it. Never reveal your walk-away line.

cards.title: Now it's a software vendor.
body: Your startup sends app emails through a vendor. At renewal they ask for 30% more and a two-year contract. Moving to another provider would take your engineers about six weeks. What's your move?

options.text: Tell them you'll switch tomorrow unless they drop the increase
options.feedback: Six weeks of migration makes this a bluff. If they call it, you lose credibility or pay anyway.

options.text: Price out the migration, then ask why two years matters to them and trade the longer term for a smaller increase
options.feedback: You know your **BATNA**, and you've found their **interest**: predictable revenue. Giving them that can buy you a lower price.

options.text: Sign the two-year deal to avoid a messy migration
options.feedback: You avoid disruption, but you lock in the higher price for two years without testing what they'd accept.

cards.title: Know your exit, then ask what they need.
body: Two ideas did the work in this lesson:
list: **Your best alternative (BATNA):** cost out what happens if talks fail, including switching costs
**Interests vs positions:** ask what's behind the number, then trade on it
cards.callout: **Try it today:** pick your biggest supplier. Write down what switching would really cost you, and one thing they might value besides price.
